title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 2311
summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia with 23 aboard (2 crew, 20 passengers, 1 flight attendant), crashed north of Brunswick, Georgia on April 5, 1991 during approach to runway 07. The NTSB investigation determined that the left propeller control unit experienced severe wear of the quill spline teeth due to the introduction of a titanium-nitrided transfer tube with harder surface characteristics. This wear allowed the left propeller to move to a near-zero blade angle, creating severe asymmetric thrust that rolled the aircraft left beyond pilot control authority. The aircraft struck trees and terrain 9,975 feet from runway 07 threshold.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the loss of control in flight as a result of a malfunction of the left engine propeller control unit which allowed the propeller blade angles to go below the flight idle position. Contributing to the accident was the deficient design of the Propeller control unit by Hamilton Standard and the approval of the design by the Federal Aviation Administration. The design did not correctly evaluate the failure mode that occurred during this flight, which resulted in an uncommanded and uncorrectable movement of the blades of the airplane's left propeller below the flight idle position.

factors.evidence: Left propeller blade angle 3 degrees with PCU commanded 79.2 degrees caused asymmetric thrust (p. 21).
Left propeller control unit malfunction allowed blade angles below flight idle (p. 21-23).
Aircraft rolled left 90 degrees and struck terrain 9,975 feet from runway (p. 9-10).
Crew completed 3 round-trip flights on consecutive days before accident flight (p. 9).

events.text: April 4, 1991: Crew began sequence of trips with round-trip flight 2284 from Atlanta to Tallahassee starting at 1319 on aircraft N228AS
Round-trip flight 2284 returned to Atlanta at 1559
Subsequent round-trip flight to Panama City completed and crew arrived at Dothan, Alabama at 2141 with flight 2173
Crew checked into hotel at 2245, ending their duty day
April 5, 1991: Captain and first officer received wake-up calls at 0515 and 0530 respectively; taxi driver reported crew in good spirits
Crew arrived at Atlanta airport by taxi at approximately 0615
Crew resumed assigned flight sequence at 0645 with flight 2101 returning to Atlanta after round-trip; round-trip to Montgomery followed
N270AS returned to Atlanta at 1042 on flight 2238; crew reported well-rested and in good spirits
Crew began scheduled rest break of 2 hours 37 minutes
Flight 2311 departed Atlanta at 1347 (23 minutes behind schedule) on aircraft N270AS; no mechanical problems noted by previous flight crews; this was fourth flight of day for this aircraft
Flight deviation around weather en route to Brunswick; arrived in Brunswick area about 1444
Flight acknowledged to Jacksonville ATC that airport was in sight; position approximately 2,300 feet above ground on radar (p. 10)
Flight 2311 cleared for visual approach to runway 07 with indicated airspeed 150 knots and heading 117 degrees magnetic (p. 10)
Flight acknowledged clearance and requested to call out of 3,000 feet direct to airport (p. 11)
Flight reported to ATC they had airport in sight on company frequency; this was last transmission known from flight 2311 (p. 9)
Left propeller blade angle began decreasing below flight idle position due to PCU quill spline disengagement from transfer tube; asymmetric thrust developed
Witnesses reported loud engine noises (squeal, whine, overspeeding) which then diminished or ceased before impact (p. 9)

Aircraft suddenly turned and rolled left until wings perpendicular to ground; descended in nose-down attitude behind trees near airport; impact 9,975 feet from runway 07 threshold at 31°15'34.8"N 81°30'34.2"W (p. 9-10)

recommendations.text: Conduct a certification review of the Hamilton Standard model 14RF propeller system and require appropriate modification to ensure compliance with 14 CFR 35.21, including vibration spectrum testing.
Examine certification basis of other propeller systems with same design characteristics as 14RF and ensure fail-safe features function properly during unforeseen wear.
Establish periodic inspection time requirement for transfer tube splines and ballscrew quill on 14RF propellers and similar systems.
Issue Air Carrier Operations Bulletin clarifying that 14 CFR 135.265 does not authorize routine reduced rest scheduling.
Discontinue scheduling of reduced rest periods; utilize reduced rest only for unexpected operational delays.
Advise members to comply with intent of 14 CFR 135.265 reduced rest provisions.

safety_changes: Hamilton Standard issued Alert Service Bulletin 14RF-9-61-A49 on May 7, 1991 requiring inspection of PCUs for worn quills and removal of titanium-nitrided transfer tubes from service (p. 30)
FAA issued emergency airworthiness directive T91-10-51 on May 9, 1991 requiring inspection of PCU ballscrew quill at maximum 500 hours with defined wear limits (p. 30-31)

FAA issued emergency airworthiness directive T91-11-51 on May 19, 1991 reducing initial inspection interval to 200 hours and reducing wear limits for repetitive inspections; terminating action was installation of original nitrided transfer tube (p. 31)

notes: Comprehensive reading of Probable Cause, Conclusions (17 findings), Recommendations (6 total), History of Flight, Loss of Propeller Control section, Propeller System testing, and design certification issues
Key failure mechanism: titanium-nitrided transfer tube coating introduced in 1990 caused accelerated wear of quill spline teeth beyond design assumptions
Design deficiency: certification testing used bright gold finish tube not representative of matted finish found in service; testing used different engine than EMB-120 certification
Fail-safe design assumption proven incorrect: propeller blade angle decreased to near-zero instead of feathering as predicted
